
The manual review of stage 1 produces two kinds of labelled clips: clips
that contain the species (positives) and clips in which the classifier
detected the species but the reviewer did not hear it (negatives). Besides
measuring precision and feeding the calibration, both can be used to
retrain the BirdNET custom classifier. This article shows how to turn the
reviewed clips into a training data set in the layout that
BirdNET-Analyzer expects, how to keep an independent set for testing the
new classifier, and what has to be redone after retraining.

Training itself runs in BirdNET-Analyzer (Python), not in R. The
requirements quoted below come from the BirdNET-Analyzer documentation
(version 2.4.0, section `birdnet_analyzer.train` of the
[command line interface](https://birdnet-team.github.io/BirdNET-Analyzer/stable/usage/cli.html));
check the version you use, since the training options change between
releases.

```{r}
library(sheepdog)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
ex <- system.file("extdata", "example", package = "sheepdog")
```

## What BirdNET-Analyzer expects

According to its documentation, the training script of BirdNET-Analyzer:

* takes a folder with **one subfolder per class**, and uses the folder
  names as labels. The recommended label format is
  `<scientific name>_<common name>`, although other formats work;
* accepts **negative samples** of a class in a folder with the same name
  prefixed by `-` (e.g. `-Boana raniceps_boa-ran`). Negative samples are
  used for training only, not for validation, and only when the folder
  with the positives of that class exists;
* treats a folder named `Noise`, `Background`, `Other` or `Silence` as a
  non-event class;
* resamples the audio to 48 kHz and works on 3 s segments;
* recommends at least 100 audio files per species, although training also
  works with fewer;
* accepts an independent test set (`--test_data`).

The documentation also states that custom classifiers trained with
BirdNET-Analyzer are licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

The clips cut by sheepdog already fit this layout: they are 3 s segments
of the original recordings, and `species_code` keeps the full label of the
classifier (`<scientific name>_<code>`), which can be used as the folder
name so that the retrained classifier reports the same labels.

## The reviewed clips

We use the reviewed clips shipped with the package. In a real project the
review is done in the Review tab of the BirdNET GUI, which moves each clip
into a `Positive` or `Negative` subfolder; here we recreate that folder
structure with empty `.wav` files from the verdicts of the example tables,
and read it back with `classify_review()`, which records where each clip
was found (`reviewed_path`).

```{r}
validation <- read_validation_tables(
  list.files(file.path(ex, "validation"), full.names = TRUE))

review_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "review")
unlink(review_dir, recursive = TRUE)
dest <- file.path(review_dir, validation$species_folder,
                  ifelse(validation$verdict == "positive",
                         "Positive", "Negative"))
for (d in unique(dest)) dir.create(d, recursive = TRUE)
invisible(file.create(file.path(dest, validation$clip_file)))

reviewed <- validation |>
  select(-verdict, -reviewed_path) |>
  classify_review(review_dir) |>
  suppressMessages()
count(reviewed, species_code, verdict)
```

`read_validation_tables()` stacks the `validation_by_clip.csv` tables of
several sites or rounds, keeping every column and verdict.

## Keeping an independent test set

A retrained classifier has to be evaluated on clips that it did not see
during training. BirdNET-Analyzer holds out a validation split
(`--val_split`) drawn from the training folder itself, but clips from the
same site and night share background noise and calling individuals, so a
random split of clips tends to overstate performance (our recommendation,
not a statement of the BirdNET documentation). A stricter test keeps whole
sites out of training and passes them as `--test_data`. Here we hold out
one site.

## Building the training folders

`build_training_set()` copies the reviewed clips into the BirdNET layout:
positives in `<set>/<species_code>/` and negatives in
`<set>/-<species_code>/`, where `<set>` is `train`, or `test` for the
sites in `test_sites`. It reads each clip from `reviewed_path`, the place
where the review left it, leaves out whole-recording clips (which have no
confidence score), writes the table of copied clips to
`training_set.csv`, and warns about classes with fewer positive training
files than `min_files` (100 by default, the number recommended by the
BirdNET documentation).

```{r}
training_root <- file.path(tempdir(), "birdnet_training")
unlink(training_root, recursive = TRUE)
training_set <- build_training_set(reviewed, training_root,
                                   test_sites = "NHE") |>
  suppressMessages()

list.files(file.path(training_root, "train"))
count(training_set, set, verdict)
```

How many positive training files each class received:

```{r}
n_pos <- training_set |>
  filter(set == "train", verdict == "positive") |>
  count(species_code) |>
  mutate(below_100 = n < 100)
n_pos
```

With the `r nrow(validation)` reviewed clips of the example,
`r sum(n_pos$below_100)` of the `r nrow(n_pos)` classes have fewer than
100 positive training files. Classes with few positives are the ones that
most need clips from further review rounds before retraining.

## Which clips to add

Three points about the composition of the training set follow from how the
clips were chosen (our recommendations, not statements of the BirdNET
documentation):

* **Clips from the `"top"` design are the easy cases.** They are the
  highest-scoring detections, so they teach the classifier little about
  the calls it currently misses or scores low. Positives from the
  `"random_detections"` and `"random_recordings"` designs (see
  `vignette("sampling-designs")`) cover lower scores and calls the
  classifier did not detect.
* **Negatives with high scores are the most informative.** They are the
  sounds the classifier confuses with the species. Species with many
  high-scoring false positives in `precision_by_bin()` (see
  `vignette("validation-effort")`) are the ones for which negatives matter
  most.
* **Whole-recording clips** of `"random_recordings"` are longer than 3 s.
  BirdNET-Analyzer crops long files (`--crop_mode`), but the label of a
  whole recording says only that the species was heard somewhere in it.
  Cut the annotated calls into 3 s clips before using them as positives.

## Training

Training runs in a Python environment with BirdNET-Analyzer installed.
The commands below follow the example of the documentation (they are not
run here):

```sh
python -m birdnet_analyzer.train birdnet_training/train \
  --test_data birdnet_training/test \
  -o checkpoints/custom/Custom_Classifier.tflite

python -m birdnet_analyzer.analyze recordings/ \
  --classifier checkpoints/custom/Custom_Classifier.tflite
```

Use `--model_format raven` (or `both`) if the classifier will also be used
in Raven. Hyperparameters such as `--hidden_units`, `--learning_rate`,
`--dropout` and the upsampling options affect the result; the
documentation recommends trying several settings, or `--autotune`.

## After retraining

A retrained classifier produces new confidence scores, so everything that
was estimated from the scores of the old one no longer applies:

1. Run the new classifier over the recordings to obtain new selection
   tables.
2. Draw and review a new set of clips (stage 1). Do not reuse the clips
   used for training: their scores are biased upwards on the data the
   classifier was trained on.
3. Recalibrate (stage 2, `vignette("calibration")`) and rebuild the
   detection histories and community matrices (stage 3).

Keep `training_set.csv` with the new classifier. Before reviewing the
detections of the retrained classifier, `exclude_training_clips()` drops
from the new manifest the clips that overlap, for the same species and
recording, a clip used in training:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
manifest_v2 <- select_clips(detections_v2, ...) |>
  exclude_training_clips(file.path(training_root, "training_set.csv"))
```

`extract_validation_clips()` records the `classifier` label in
`extraction_info.csv`, so each validation round can be traced to the
classifier that produced its clips.
